Q: The pointer existential crisis dilemma: If pointer stores memory address then how are memory addresses of a pointers stored? A:

Pointers are objects as any other objects of other types. You may take an address of any object that is not a temporary object or is not declared with storage class specifier register.

Consider the following declaration

T x;

where T is a type.

When you can declare a pointer that points to this variable

T *p = &x;

Now you can define the type T as for example

typedef int *T;

In this case the type of the pointer p will be T *. That is for the variable p the program allocates memory of the size sizeof( p ) and stores there the value of the address of the variable x.

The type T can be defined in turn as a pointer type as for example

typedef int ***T;

In this case the variable x itself will have the pointer type int * and the variable p will have a pointer to to pointer type that is int ****. The memory for pointers are allocated the same way as for other scalar types.

Q: Whats the difference between a SVG file and a md file? A:

SVG and MD are just two file formats with fundamentally different intentions.

Markdown is intended to represent text and to format the text a bit, while keeping the 'source-code' still readable as text.
SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) on the other hand is intended to describe graphics, in which text and text-formatting would rather be a side-effect, than the original intention.

So generally speaking, Markdown would be the choice to write text, while SVG would be the choice to create images.
